messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 22
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Product Manager
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 36

# The Weight of What He Saw

Miguel is twenty-two years old, the youngest product manager at a mid-sized tech startup in Austin, Texas. His colleagues know him as sharp, driven, and unusually composed for someone his age. What they do not know is that he spent three weeks two years ago trapped in his grandmother's house in a northern region of Venezuela while armed conflict between government forces and paramilitary groups tore through the neighborhood around him.

He had gone back to visit family during a long holiday weekend — a trip he had made before without incident. Within days of his arrival, the streets outside became impassable. He remembers the specific afternoon it started: the sound of automatic gunfire so close it rattled the windowpanes, his grandmother pulling him to the floor of the kitchen, the smell of her hair and the tile cold against his cheek. Over the following weeks, he watched a neighbor's house burn. He saw a man he did not recognize lying motionless in the road for two full days before anyone came for him. He heard things at night he still cannot name. When he finally made it to the airport and boarded a plane back to the United States, he told himself it was over.

It was not over.

For the first several months after returning, Miguel threw himself into work with an intensity that his supervisors mistook for ambition. He was the first one in, the last to leave, filling every quiet moment with tasks and Slack messages and roadmap spreadsheets. Stillness, he discovered, was dangerous. When he sat still, the sounds came back — not as memories exactly, but as physical sensations, a tightening in his chest, a sudden certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He stopped sleeping in his bedroom and began falling asleep on his couch with the television on, needing the noise to hold the silence at bay.

Now, two years later, the coping strategies that once worked are fraying. He lives in a one-bedroom apartment alone and keeps the blinds drawn most evenings. He has not been back to visit his family, and he deflects his mother's questions about when he will return with vague talk about deadlines and product launches. He avoids the news entirely — not just Venezuelan news, but all of it. A coworker played a video clip of a protest in the break room last month and Miguel left the room so abruptly that he had to spend ten minutes in the bathroom talking himself back to baseline before returning to his desk.

He is not sleeping well. He wakes at two or three in the morning, heart already racing, reaching for something to orient himself. He rarely remembers the dreams, only the feeling they leave behind — a residue of dread that follows him into the morning. He has become irritable in ways that embarrass him, snapping at colleagues during sprint reviews over small things, then spending the rest of the day quietly ashamed of himself. He is aware that something is wrong. He is not sure he deserves to call it that.

This last part is perhaps what weighs on him most. He is alive. He is employed. He has a future laid out in front of him in a country where he is safe. He was not a soldier. He was not a refugee. He was a visitor who got caught in something terrible and then got out. He tells himself this often, as though repetition might dissolve what he carries. It does not. He came to his first therapy session wearing a collared shirt, speaking carefully and precisely, the way he might present a product roadmap. But when the therapist asked him what it had been like to finally board that plane out of Venezuela, he went quiet for a long moment, looked down at his hands, and said, very softly, that he still does not quite believe he made it.
